Parvati Is a Classic Italian Icon Disguised as a Bargain
28 photos
Photo: Worth Avenue Yachts
With the 67th edition of the Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show currently underway, we are reminded that so many spectacular luxury yachts in all size categories continue to appear and dazzle, adding new excitement to the market. Still, even with all of these superb luxury toys turning heads, there will always be a special place for classics, and nothing beats a true Italian classic like Parvati.
At face value, the preference for classic yachts could be considered simply a matter of taste. Connoisseurs will appreciate their quirks and even their faults, and many of them are willing to spend millions, sometime even more that what they paid for the yacht itself, to restore its classic beauty and make sure it remains seaworthy for the next decades.
Others might find classic yachts from certain eras, like the ‘70s and ‘80s, to look tacky and certainly outdated. While technologically they can be proven travelers, rugged enough to be even more reliable than younger counterparts, classic yachts have a distinctive style that people either love or hate.
Parvati falls in the same category. Some will immediately appreciate its classic gentleman’s yacht silhouette and ‘80s exterior styling, while others will only see it as a project that needs full rehabilitation. The truth is that Parvati has been searching for a new owner for quite a while. Back in 2024, it was listed for sale almost in the same condition as today, and for the same price: €2.35 million. Today, that’s the equivalent of roughly $2.6 million.
Photo: Worth Avenue Yachts It’s a bargain, considering that Parvati is presented in excellent shape, ready to sail, and upgraded following several refits. Yes, its classic ‘80s interiors haven’t really changed over the years, and perhaps they could benefit from a major transformation, but as far as performance goes (which is the most important), Parvati is in top shape.
At the time of its launch, in 1979, this Italian icon was named Santa Cruz Tres. Over the decades, its name changed multiple times, indicating several ownerships. It was never linked by the media to a famous or particularly wealthy owner, which is probably why Parvati stayed in the shadows compared to other CRN yachts from the same era. Still, its discretion doesn’t mean a lack of style.
Parvati showcases the well-known Italian elegance of the early ‘80s era in full glory, and its beautiful silhouette is a reflection of the CRN heritage – one of the most significant names in Italian yacht-building. It was the result of a collaboration between CRN and the Kirschstein Designs for exterior and interior design.
Size-wise, Parvati is not a superyacht, but closer to a classic gentleman’s yacht. An overall length of almost 110 feet (38 meters) is coupled with a 23-foot (7.1 meters) beam, an 8.5-foot (3.4 meters) draft, and internal volume of 239 GT. A classic steel hull with an aluminum superstructure strikes a balance between robustness and speed.
Photo: Worth Avenue Yachts Two CAT engines (1,200 hp) propel Parvati at a cruising speed of 12 knots, and a maximum speed of almost 15 knots. At an eco-speed of 10.5 knots, this smaller yacht can ensure a range of 5,000 nautical miles, enough for a wide range of destinations.
Throughout the years, Parvati has undergone several refits, but the most important one in its history is the 1999 visit to the French shipyard La Ciotat, where it was practically rebuilt. That is the year that marks the difference between the original Santa Cruz Tres era and the modern Parvati. Many years later, in 2014, it would undergo another comprehensive refit.
Today, as well as in 2024, when it joined the market, no other recent refits are mentioned, except for new teak added to the side decks in 2019.
Despite this being a yacht below 50 meters, it offers a similar accommodation capacity to much bigger superyachts. The difference is that it doesn’t have the same ultra-spacious outdoor areas; back then, in the early ‘80s, when the era of superyachts was just starting, owners didn’t put such an emphasis on outdoor living as today, when it’s one of the top requests for any new yacht design.
Photo: Worth Avenue Yachts Parvati can comfortably welcome 10 to 11 guests in five staterooms. The master suite has the traditional placement on the main deck, and it includes a walk-in wardrobe, a makeup vanity, and an en-suite bathroom with a bathtub and two sinks. All the guest staterooms are located on the lower deck, and two of them can be connected into a single full-beam suite, thanks to a sliding partition.
Back in the day, before designers truly mastered the outdoor living area onboard superyachts, the main salon was the most important area for socializing onboard a yacht. Parvati’s classic main salon stands out due to the 2.1-meter (6.9 feet) ceiling height, which is generous for that era, and a big influence on the overall ambiance of the salon.
In addition to the comfortable seating, there’s enough space for a huge dining area, big enough for all ten guests. The separate TV lounge, fully glass-enclosed and with expansive views of the water, is the classic and humbler format of what is called a media room today – basically, a more intimate space for socializing and relaxation.
Although modest compared to a modern superyacht’s features, Parvati offers its own kind of outdoor fun, including al-fresco dining for up to eight guests in a dedicated, shaded area on the aft deck. On the flybridge, guests have access to the traditional sun lounging area, a bar, and a barbecue.
Photo: Worth Avenue Yachts The flybridge also houses the yacht’s tender and two Jet Skis, which frees up the aft deck for al-fresco dining. There’s also no spacious beach club, just a simple swim platform for direct access to the water.
Above everything else, Parvati is one of the rare representatives of an important stage in the history of the Italian CRN shipyard. In the early ‘70s, CRN yachts gained the distinctive features that would become the brand’s signature. A bow shape inspired by fishing boats and unusual at the time became the trademark of CRN yachts, although it was mainly introduced for practical reasons, including greater safety in choppy seas.
Santa Cruz Tres was one of the memorable yachts built in that era, from the early ‘70s to the beginning of the ‘80s, alongside names like Gazzella (1974), Moneikos (1976), and Varmar (1982). One of the most emblematic CRN yachts of that same era was Fath al Khair, the 74-meter yacht custom-built for the Emir of Quatar in 1978.
In the following era, from the ‘80’s to the ‘90s, CRN would go on to build and launch one of the most innovative and impressive yachts of its time: the legendary F110, owned by Gianni Agnelli (head of Fiat and Ferrari, and one of the most important figures in Italy’s contemporary history).
Photo: Worth Avenue Yachts The F110 is considered by experts one of the ancestors of contemporary explorer superyachts. It was the first yacht ever to include floating rubber supports for lower noise levels, and anti-vibration tiles. It was the first of its size (33 meters) to have a heliport, and it was purposely beefed-up for extended cruising in the harshest weather conditions and at all latitudes.
Although not as legendary as the F110, this earlier CRN is still a collector’s item for those who appreciate classic Italian yacht design and the advantages of a smaller, slimmer yacht. Now asking $2.6 million, Parvati is worth grabbing for an elevated cruising experience in classic style.
